title: A sorted ascending array of distinct integers has been rotated at some unknown pivot. Find the minimum element in logarithmic time.
shortTitle: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array: Binary Search on the Inflection Point
keyPoints: The minimum element in a rotated sorted array sits at the single inflection point where the sequence drops.
Compare the middle element with the rightmost element to decide which half contains the minimum.
If arr[mid] > arr[high], the inflection is to the right, so set low = mid + 1.
If arr[mid] <= arr[high], mid could be the minimum or the minimum is to its left, so set high = mid.
Use the loop condition while (low < high) and set high = mid, not mid - 1, to avoid skipping the answer.
Comparing against the right endpoint handles the non-rotated case naturally.
With duplicates, arr[mid] == arr[high] is ambiguous and forces high-- which degrades to O(n) worst case.

s1_definition.oneliner: Compare the middle element to the rightmost element to determine which half contains the inflection point where the minimum lives.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Inflection point** – a rotated sorted array has two ascending runs with one drop between them; the minimum is the start of the second run.
- **Decision rule** – if `arr[mid] > arr[high]`, the drop is strictly to the right of mid, so `low = mid + 1`; otherwise the drop is at mid or to its left, so `high = mid`.
- **Loop condition** – use `while (low < high)` because we are converging two pointers to a single index, not matching a value.
- **Right anchor** – comparing against `arr[high]` rather than `arr[low]` naturally handles the non-rotated case where the minimum is at index zero.
- **Time complexity** – O(log n) with distinct values; O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India logs daily closing balances sorted ascending across a cycle, but the reporting system starts from an arbitrary day, which rotates the sorted sequence. The risk team needs the minimum balance fast. The clerk opens the ledger in the middle and compares the middle balance to the last balance to tell which side the drop is on, then repeats on that side until the minimum is found.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the minimum in a rotated sorted array is a binary search on the inflection point, the single place where the sequence drops from a high value back to the smallest value. A rotated sorted array of distinct values is really two ascending runs with one drop between them, and the minimum is exactly the start of the second run.

The decision at each step is simple: compare the middle element to the rightmost element. If the middle is greater than the right end, the drop must lie strictly to the right of the middle, so you move low to mid plus one. Otherwise the middle could itself be the minimum or the minimum is to its left, so you move high to mid, deliberately not mid minus one, because you must keep the middle in the window as a candidate. You loop while low is strictly less than high, and when they meet, that single index holds the minimum.

In Rajesh's work at the National Bank of India, the risk team logs end-of-day balances in ascending order across a cycle, but the reporting system stores them starting from an arbitrary day, which rotates the sorted sequence. The team needs the minimum balance quickly to flag whether it ever dipped dangerously low, and this inflection-point search finds it logarithmically instead of scanning every day.

The two correctness points to always highlight are the strict less-than loop condition with high set to mid, which prevents both infinite loops and stepping over the answer, and the choice to anchor on the right endpoint, which handles the non-rotated case cleanly without extra code. The duplicate-values variant introduces an ambiguous case where mid equals high, forcing a linear fallback, and knowing exactly when that happens shows real understanding.

Remember one sentence: compare mid to the right end and always move toward the side where the drop must be, converging on the minimum in O(log n) time.
